title: Origin of primates
summary: Plesiadapiforms, an extinct group of stem primates, first appear in the fossil record shortly after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. Purgatorius, the oldest of them, lived in what is now northeastern Montana about 65.9 million years ago. It was a small mammal eating fruit and insects, and its ankle bones show that it lived in trees.

uncertainty.note: Start is the early Puercan occurrence of Purgatorius at Harley's Point in Montana (65.946–65.912 Ma); end is the Paleocene-Eocene thermal maximum transition when crown euprimates dispersed globally.

as_recorded.calendar: geological time (Royal Society Open Science / PMC8074693)

where.modern_name: Northeastern Montana, United States (earliest known fossils)
where.historical_name: Interior subtropical forests of North America, early Paleocene; no polities existed

importance.justification: The origin of primates established the grasping extremities, arboreal agility, stereoscopic vision, and expanded neocortex that underpinned the evolutionary lineage of anthropoids, apes, and humans.

related.because: The mass extinction of non-avian dinosaurs cleared arboreal canopy niches that facilitated the rapid diversification of plesiadapiform stem primates.
The Triassic emergence of mammals established the mammalian body plan and placental lineage from which primates arose.
The Paleocene primate radiation gave rise to the anthropoid lineages that later diversified in Afro-Arabia at Fayum.
The primate lineage founded in the early Paleocene ultimately led through hominoids and hominins to the genus Homo.
